question: According to their notion of kingship, many Kushana rulers adopted the title of ________.
solution:
The correct answer is __**Devaputra**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] __Key Points__

__
 
• The title **Devaputra** translates to "Son of God," emphasizing the divine legitimacy of the ruler.
 
• It was prominently used by Kushana rulers, especially **Kanishka I**, to highlight their connection to divine authority.
 
• The adoption of such a title was influenced by the integration of Indian, Iranian, and Hellenistic cultural elements in the Kushana Empire.
 
• The Kushana rulers were known for their syncretic approach, blending various religious and cultural traditions to legitimize their rule over a diverse population.
 
• This title also reflects the influence of Buddhism, as the Kushanas were great patrons of Buddhist art, culture, and philosophy.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

 
• **Kanishka I:**

 
 
• One of the most famous Kushana rulers, known for his contributions to art, trade, and the spread of Buddhism.
 
• He convened the **Fourth Buddhist Council** in Kashmir, which played a key role in the development of Mahayana Buddhism.
 
 
 
• **Kushana Empire:**
 
 
• A powerful empire in Central and South Asia during the 1st to 3rd centuries CE.
 
• It controlled major trade routes, including the Silk Road, facilitating cultural and economic exchange.
 
 
 
• **Religious Patronage:**
 
 
• The Kushanas supported multiple religions, including Buddhism, Hinduism, and Zoroastrianism.
 
• Their coins and inscriptions often depicted deities from these traditions, reflecting their inclusive policies.
 
 
 
• **Art and Architecture:**
 
 
• The Kushanas were instrumental in the development of the Gandhara and Mathura schools of art.
 
• These art forms combined Greco-Roman, Indian, and Central Asian influences, leading to the creation of iconic Buddhist sculptures.
